candidate_relations.reason: The patient has diffuse GI polyposis consistent with juvenile polyposis, but the onychodystrophy, brownish macules, hyperchromic punctate lesions, and severe malabsorption point specifically to Cronkhite-Canada syndrome. Juvenile polyposis does not account for the ectodermal manifestations.
candidate_relations.scope_detail: Juvenile polyposis syndrome shares GI polyposis but lacks the ectodermal triad (alopecia, onychodystrophy, skin pigmentation) and protein-losing enteropathy that define Cronkhite-Canada syndrome; also typically hereditary

candidate_relations.reason: This is a direct transliteration/translation of the reference diagnosis. All required components (diffuse GI polyposis, ectodermal changes including onychodystrophy and skin pigmentation, protein-losing enteropathy with hypoalbuminemia and micronutrient deficiencies) are captured by this label.
candidate_relations.scope_detail: Cronkhite-Canada综合征 is the Chinese-language rendering of Cronkhite-Canada syndrome — identical diagnostic entity

candidate_relations.reason: The clinical picture is dominated by diffuse GI polyposis and ectodermal manifestations (onychodystrophy, pigmented macules), which are not features of autoimmune enteropathy. Endoscopy showed polyps, not villous atrophy or autoimmune mucosal injury.
candidate_relations.scope_detail: Autoimmune enteropathy is a distinct entity characterized by immune-mediated villous atrophy without the polyposis or ectodermal features seen here

candidate_relations.reason: While the brownish macules on hands/feet could superficially suggest Peutz-Jeghers, the polyp distribution (gastric, duodenal, colonic — not predominantly small bowel), onychodystrophy, hyperchromic truncal lesions, and severe hypoalbuminemia/zinc deficiency are inconsistent with Peutz-Jeghers and instead fit Cronkhite-Canada syndrome.
candidate_relations.scope_detail: Peutz-Jeghers syndrome shares mucocutaneous pigmentation and GI polyposis but involves hamartomatous polyps with distinct histology, STK11 mutation, and does not cause onychodystrophy or the protein-losing enteropathy pattern seen here

case_quality_flags: Atypical age presentation: Cronkhite-Canada syndrome classically affects middle-aged to elderly adults; a 15-year-old is exceptionally rare and may warrant additional diagnostic scrutiny
Alopecia not explicitly mentioned in the record, though onychodystrophy and skin changes are documented — the classic ectodermal triad is only partially described
